text.p: Dressed from head to toe in blue and yellow, few would dispute that young Brazilian Gustavo Kuerten is the most colourful player at this year's French Open.

But in a city which requires a dress code to wash your car, the fashion-conscious Parisians aren't quite sure what to make of the long-haired 20-year-old, the first Brazilian in 29 years to reach the quarter-finals of this grand slam tournament.
The Roland Garros fashion police have already made it clear what they think about Kuerten's colourful attire -- not much.

Down at 66th place in the world rankings, Kuerten's appearance in the final eight was so unexpected that French Open officials neglected to talk to the Brazilian about the boundaries of taste as they did to his quarter-final opponent, defending champion Yevgeny Kafelnikov, who is sponsored by the same clothing compay.
"The director of the tournament came and asked me to change my clothes," said Kuerten, who lists surfing and soccer among his favourite pastimes away from the court.
"I think he (the tournament director) talked to our clothing company and asked them to put a little white on (Kafelnikov's) clothes.
"He told me he didn't expect me to go too far so that's why he didn't talk to them about me.
"They said they don't mind it here if the players wear blue, yellow or green but that you shouldn't be all blue and yellow like me.
"I have nothing white. I have yellow socks, blue shoes -- at least my underwear is white."

Unless he hears otherwise from his clothing sponsor, Kuerten said he would at least wear a white headband in his quarter-final clash against Kafelnikov but added he would be dressed in traditional whites when he makes his first appearance at Wimbledon later this month.
"I have to play with these clothes, I have no more clothes to play in," said Kuerten. "I promised him I would wear a bandana in white, that's all I have said."
